library(jsonlite)

read_json_file <- function (arg0_path) {
  txt <- readLines(arg0_path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  fromJSON(paste(txt, collapse = "\n"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json_file("india_after_independence.json5")
set_data <- read_json_file("india_after_independence_settlements.json")

clean_text <- function (arg0_s) {
  s <- gsub("&", "and", as.character(arg0_s), fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("_", " ", s, fixed = TRUE)
  trimws(s)
}

fmt_yr <- function (arg0_y) {
  y <- as.numeric(arg0_y)
  if (y < 0) return(paste0(abs(round(y)), "BC"))
  return(paste0(round(y), "AD"))
}

# Abstract

The Republic of India (encompassing 3.129.521 km² and 39.932 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells) underwent the largest peacetime demographic expansion in human history during the eight decades following independence in August 1947. From an initial post-Partition population of 344M in 1947AD, enumerated at 361,09M in the foundational 1951AD census, regional population grew at more than 2% annually during the middle decennia of the twentieth century, reaching 548,16M in 1971AD, surpassing one billion at 1.028,74M in 2001AD and attaining 1.210,85M in 2011AD. Reconstructed across eight administrative and physiographic divisions under INDUS, contemporary population reaches 1,47B in 2026AD (yielding an aggregate density of 468,12 persons per km²). This demographic surge reflected a dramatic collapse in crude death rates and infant mortality driven by post-war public health programmes, malaria eradication, famine control and agrarian expansion, while total fertility rates remained elevated above 5,5 children per woman through the 1960s before embarking upon a prolonged, regionally uneven decline.

The geographic manifestation of this transition was marked by profound regional divergence between northern and southern states. The southern peninsular states (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana) led the national transition, with Kerala reaching sub-replacement fertility by 1988AD and Tamil Nadu following in the early 1990s, stabilising the southern demographic share at 19,4% in 2026AD (284,21M inhabitants; 447,89 persons per km²). In contrast, the northern Hindi heartland across the alluvial plains of Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Bihar and Jharkhand experienced sustained momentum, expanding more than fourfold from 103,2M in 1947AD to 439,5M in 2026AD, attaining an extraordinary regional density of 950,51 persons per km² and accounting for 30% of national population. The western industrial belt of Maharashtra and Gujarat grew from 49,88M to 212,43M, while the northwest expanded from 44,72M to 190,45M, anchored by the rapid metropolitan expansion of Delhi from 1,44M in 1951AD to 19,86M inhabitants in 2025AD.

Urbanisation proceeded through dual modalities of metropolitan concentration and in situ rural transformation. Alongside primary metropolises such as Mumbai (18,39M in 2011AD; 22,35M in 2025AD), Delhi (16,35M in 2011AD; 19,86M in 2025AD), Kolkata (14,06M in 2011AD; 17,08M in 2025AD), Chennai (8,65M in 2011AD; 10,51M in 2025AD) and Bengaluru (8,52M in 2011AD; 10,35M in 2025AD), the post-1991 period witnessed a rapid expansion of sub-metropolitan census towns and intermediate market centres that absorbed agricultural labour surpluses. This study integrates decennial census schedules, Sample Registration System vital registers and 28.538 georeferenced settlements anchored in Census of India Table A-04 records, primary-monograph metropolis trajectories, multi-repository archaeological corpora and macro-envelope continuity chains with 5-arcminute dasymetric surfaces. Settlement subtraction isolates nucleated urban populations from dasymetrically distributed rural cultivators, establishing a quantitative baseline for South Asian population history and tracking the closing phases of India's demographic dividend.

# Background

## Historical Demography at Independence and Partition

The birth of independent India in August 1947 was accompanied by monumental human displacement and demographic disruption [@Hasmot2015India]. The Radcliffe partition of British India severed the contiguous alluvial plains of Punjab and Bengal, precipitating the forced migration of approximately fifteen million people across international frontiers and causing between 500k and one million violent deaths [@Yaseen2016Pakistan; @Gill2019Global]. In northwestern India, incoming Hindu and Sikh refugees transformed the demographic profile of East Punjab, Haryana and Delhi, turning the former imperial capital into an overcrowded city of displaced persons camps before state-sponsored resettlement schemes laid the foundations for suburban expansion [@Hasmot2015India]. In eastern India, Partition severed the jute hinterland of East Bengal from the processing mills of Kolkata, initiating waves of refugee migration into West Bengal, Assam and Tripura that continued across subsequent decades, particularly during the Bangladesh Liberation War of 1971AD [@Yaseen2016Pakistan; @Badgujar2017Insurgency].

The initial post-independence enumeration, the Census of 1951AD, recorded a national population of 361.088.090 inhabitants within the newly defined borders of the Union [@Hasmot2015India]. This baseline reflected centuries of high-mortality equilibrium: life expectancy at birth in 1951AD stood at merely 32,1 years, the crude death rate hovered near 27,4 per thousand and infant mortality exceeded 145 per thousand live births [@Kumar2017Health]. The rural economy remained overwhelmingly dominant, with 82,7% of the workforce engaged in agrarian subsistence and less than 17,3% residing in designated urban settlements [@Jain2018Contempo].

## The Mortality Transition and Public Health Interventions

The primary catalyst for India's post-independence population explosion was an abrupt collapse in mortality unaccompanied by an immediate decline in fertility [@Kumar2017Health; @James2026Silent]. Beginning in the early 1950s under the First and Second Five-Year Plans, the national government mounted large-scale vertical public health campaigns. The National Malaria Eradication Programme, launched in 1953AD with international assistance, deployed widespread DDT spraying across hyper-endemic alluvial and forested zones, drastically reducing malaria incidence from an estimated 75M clinical cases in 1947AD to under 100k cases by the mid-1960s [@Kumar2017Health].

Concurrently, public vaccination campaigns suppressed epidemic smallpox, cholera and plague, while investments in primary health centres, rural water supply and antibiotic therapies curtailed infectious mortality [@Kumar2017Health; @Pradeep2016Making]. Improved famine relief logistics and the expansion of the Public Distribution System prevented catastrophic mortality spikes during drought years, terminating the recurrent mortality shocks that had decimated nineteenth-century populations. As a consequence, crude death rates plummeted from 27,4 per thousand in 1951AD to 14,9 in 1971AD and 7,1 per thousand by 2011AD, while life expectancy at birth rose to 49,7 years by 1971AD and approached 70 years by 2021AD [@Kumar2017Health; @Jain2025Populati].

Because crude birth rates remained near 40 per thousand through the 1950s and 1960s, the widening gap between births and deaths triggered an acceleration in natural increase. Annual population growth accelerated from 1,25% in the 1940s to 1,96% in the 1950s, peaking at 2,22% per annum during the 1960s and 1970s [@Chakraborty2020What; @Gudaganavar2012Demograp]. This expansion generated an expansive young age structure, laying the biological groundwork for multi-decade demographic momentum.

## Agrarian Modernisation and Regional Divergence

The spatial distribution of demographic growth was strongly conditioned by regional variations in agricultural ecology and state investment [@Soudatti2023Management]. Facing severe grain shortages and foreign exchange crises in the mid-1960s, the Indian state implemented the Green Revolution strategy, concentrating high-yielding semi-dwarf wheat and rice varieties, synthetic nitrogen fertilisers and tubewell irrigation in regions possessing reliable water control [@Soudatti2023Management; @Manish2019Greater]. Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh became the primary beneficiaries of this transformation, achieving massive gains in agricultural productivity that absorbed rural labour and supported dense agrarian settlement networks.

In contrast, rain-fed and semi-arid tracts in the Deccan plateau, central India and eastern tribal uplands experienced slower productivity growth, exacerbating regional disparities in rural incomes and nutritional security [@Soudatti2023Management; @Manpreet2017Strong]. Agrarian commercialisation in western and southern states stimulated agro-processing industries, including cooperative sugar mills in western Maharashtra and dairy networks in Gujarat, which fostered dynamic secondary market towns and diversified rural employment [@Soudatti2023Management].

## The Divergent Demographic Transition: Peninsular Decline versus Northern Momentum

By the 1980s, India's national demographic trajectory fractured into two starkly divergent geographic regimes [@Konita2026Fertility; @James2026Silent]. The southern peninsular states initiated an early and rapid fertility transition that defied traditional socioeconomic development models. Kerala achieved replacement-level fertility (total fertility rate of 2,1) by 1988AD, followed closely by Tamil Nadu in the early 1990s, and subsequently Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka [@James2026Silent; @Ghosh2017Second]. This southern transition was driven by high female literacy, progressive land reforms, accessible primary healthcare, active family planning outreach and low infant mortality, rather than rapid industrialisation or high per capita income [@James2026Silent; @Pradeep2016Making].

Conversely, the populous northern states of the Hindi heartland (historically designated as the BIMARU group: Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh) experienced prolonged high fertility [@Konita2026Fertility; @Gupta2023Demograp]. Total fertility rates in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar remained above 4 children per woman well into the 1990s, held up by low female educational attainment, early marriage, strong patriarchal kinship structures and son preference [@Konita2026Fertility; @Chopkar2024Demograp]. Even in major eastern metropolitan centres such as Kolkata, fertility compressed to lowest-low levels below 1,5 while surrounding rural districts retained elevated fertility [@Ghosh2017Second]. This regional bifurcation reshaped the national demographic map, concentrating an expanding majority of India's youthful workforce in northern states while the southern peninsula confronted premature population ageing and tightening labour supplies [@Jain2025Populati; @Neelannavar2026Transformi; @Khirwar2023Interpla].

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To model demographic density surfaces across 3.129.521 km² of national territory, the INDUS spatial framework partitions India into 39.932 active terrestrial grid cells at 5-arcminute resolution (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at tropical latitudes). Each terrestrial cell is evaluated against environmental covariates:
- Perennial hydrography: Euclidean distance to perennial river systems (Ganga, Yamuna, Brahmaputra, Indus tributaries, Narmada, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) and major irrigation canals, with density attenuation modelled beyond 20 km in arid zones [@Patel2026India; @Rani2026Recapping].
- Topographic slope: terrain penalty functions derived from digital elevation data, dampening densities across the high Himalaya, Karakoram, Western Ghats and eastern tribal hill ranges while favouring alluvial plains and coastal deltas.
- Bioclimatic moisture: annual rainfall gradients derived from meteorological reanalyses, distinguishing arid western Rajasthan (< 300 mm) from monsoon-drenched coastal Kerala and the Brahmaputra valley (> 2.500 mm).
- Agricultural land cover: remote sensing inventories of net cultivated area, double-cropped alluvium and canal command tracts.

## Decennial Census Ingestion and Boundary Harmonisation

Historical demographic data were extracted from the decennial censuses of India spanning 1951AD through 2011AD [@Genadek2022Measurin]. Because Indian state and district boundaries underwent repeated administrative reorganisations (notably the States Reorganisation Act of 1956AD, the bifurcation of Bombay State in 1960AD, the division of Punjab in 1966AD and the creation of Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Uttarakhand in 2000AD), historical census district counts were harmonised onto invariant geographic polygons matching the eight INDUS macro-regions.

For the post-2011 period, during which the scheduled 2021AD decennial census was postponed due to the COVID-19 pandemic, benchmark figures for 2021AD (1,4B) and 2026AD (1,47B) were established using official projections from the National Commission on Population, Sample Registration System fertility and mortality series, and electoral roll registrations [@Team2019Imperative; @Jain2025Populati].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To eliminate double counting between nucleated urban agglomerations and rural cultivators, 28.538 catalogued settlements possessing WGS84 coordinates and longitudinal population series were compiled from the Census of India Table A-04 Class I to VI records, South Asian primary-monograph metropolis series [@Habib1982Atlas; @Moosvi1987Economy; @Bayly1983Rulers; @ImperialGazetteer1908], multi-repository archaeological and heritage corpora (Pleiades, Zenodo Harappan, Vidarbha and Palaeolithic IAR compilations, ASI P1371, Wikidata, OpenStreetMap and XRONOS/c14bazAAR), GeoNames South Asia, and macro-envelope qasba, pargana and nadu continuity chains [@Hambly1982Towns; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade; @Stein1989Vijayanagara; @Eaton1993Rise].

At each benchmark year, the aggregate population of active catalogued towns within each sub-region is computed and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope:
$$P_{\text{rural}, r}(t) = P_{\text{total}, r}(t) - \sum_{s \in S_r} P_{s}(t)$$
The residual rural population $P_{\text{rural}, r}(t)$ is subsequently distributed across non-settled rural pixels in proportion to environmental suitability weights. A two-pass boundary feathering kernel smoothes density transitions across sub-regional borders, preventing artificial step discontinuities along state boundaries.

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Every sub-regional and macro-regional benchmark estimate incorporates explicit symmetric uncertainty bounds (+/- 4% in 1947AD, +/- 1,5% across official census years from 1951AD to 2011AD, and +/- 2,5% for contemporary 2021AD and 2026AD projections). In 2026AD, the national population of 1,47B is bounded between 1.428,38M and 1.501,62M inhabitants. These intervals accommodate minor census under-enumeration in remote tribal tracts, informal urban settlement dwellers and post-2011 projection variances [@Genadek2022Measurin; @Gupta2023Demograp].

Table \ref{tab:subregions} documents the eight macro-regions, land areas, benchmark populations and 2026AD densities.

```{r tbl-subregions, results='asis'}
sub_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  r <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  a <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  p_1947 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1947"]])
  p_1961 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1961"]])
  p_1981 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1981"]])
  p_2001 <- as.numeric(r$population[["2001"]])
  p_2011 <- as.numeric(r$population[["2011"]])
  p_2026 <- as.numeric(r$population[["2026"]])
  dens_2026 <- p_2026 / a
  data.frame(
    Region = if (!is.null(reg_short[[rk]])) reg_short[[rk]] else clean_text(r$name),
    Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(a, 0L), " (", viscount_fmt_number(a / tot_area * 100, 1L), "%)"),
    P1947 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1947),
    P1961 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1961),
    P1981 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1981),
    P2001 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_2001),
    P2011 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_2011),
    P2026 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_2026),
    Density2026 = viscount_fmt_number(dens_2026, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sub <- do.call(rbind, sub_rows)
df_tot <- data.frame(
  Region = "National Total",
  Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(tot_area, 0L), " (100%)"),
  P1947 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1947),
  P1961 = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1961"]]),
  P1981 = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1981"]]),
  P2001 = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["2001"]]),
  P2011 = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["2011"]]),
  P2026 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_2026),
  Density2026 = viscount_fmt_number(tot_2026 / tot_area, 2L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_sub <- rbind(df_sub, df_tot)
viscount_table(
  df_sub,
  "Macro-regional land area, benchmark populations and 2026AD density across the Republic of India.",
  c("Macro-Region", "Area km² (Share)", "1947AD", "1961AD", "1981AD", "2001AD", "2011AD", "2026AD", "2026AD Density"),
  list(label = "tab:subregions", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Testing and Validation

## Vital Registration and Sample Registration System Cross-Checks

Because civil registration of births and deaths remained incomplete across much of rural India throughout the twentieth century, the Office of the Registrar General established the Sample Registration System (SRS) in 1969AD to provide dual-record vital estimates [@Genadek2022Measurin; @Kumar2017Health]. The demographic trajectories reconstructed here were cross-checked against quinquennial SRS total fertility rates, crude birth rates and crude death rates across major states.

The SRS time series corroborate the timing of fertility deceleration across regions: national total fertility declined from 5,2 in 1971AD to 4,5 in 1981AD, 3,6 in 1991AD, 3,1 in 2001AD, 2,4 in 2011AD and 2,0 by 2021AD, dipping slightly below replacement level nationally [@Konita2026Fertility; @James2026Silent]. The close alignment between integrated census counts and SRS natural increase estimates confirms that our intercensal growth trajectories accurately track biological demographic fundamentals.

## Satellite Remote Sensing and Built-Up Surface Detection

To validate urban settlement boundaries and rural dasymetric distributions, high-resolution earth observation datasets, including the Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL) and Nighttime Lights from DMSP-OLS and VIIRS, were evaluated against catalogued urban nodes [@Jain2018Contempo]. Satellite multi-spectral imagery demonstrates that built-up surface area expanded at more than twice the rate of urban population growth after 1990AD, reflecting rapid horizontal peri-urban sprawl around Tier-1 and Tier-2 cities [@Jain2018Contempo].

Furthermore, satellite observations confirm the emergence of dense ribbon developments along major transport corridors (such as the Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor and the Grand Trunk Road axis across the Gangetic plain), validating our road-proximity weighting in rural dasymetric allocation [@Jain2018Contempo; @Manish2019Greater].

## Demographic Dividend and Age-Structural Validations

The age structural transition of India's population has been widely analysed in the economic literature to evaluate the magnitude of the demographic dividend [@Jain2025Populati; @Chakraborty2020What; @Gudaganavar2012Demograp]. Between 1971AD and 2021AD, the proportion of the population in the dependent age groups (under 15 years) contracted from 42% to 25,3%, while the working-age population (ages 15 to 64) expanded from 53,4% to 67,5% [@Jain2025Populati; @Khirwar2023Interpla]. This transition drove the national age dependency ratio down from 0,87 in 1971AD to 0,48 in 2021AD.

Comparative analyses with China and other transitioning economies demonstrate that while China leveraged its demographic window through aggressive export manufacturing and rapid rural-to-urban transition, India realised a more modest economic dividend due to constraints in secondary education, female labour force participation and formal industrial employment [@Gupta2023Demograp; @Cai2010Demograp; @Budiansky1984Chinese; @Qin2026Scenario]. Studies of similar demographic transitions in the Middle East and Africa reinforce the finding that capturing the demographic dividend requires timely investments in human capital and employment creation [@Islam2020Demograp; @Mbaye2023Fertilit; @Chopkar2024Demograp; @Neelannavar2026Transformi].

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The INDUS source ledger was assembled through a four-wave saturation ingestion methodology:
- Wave 1: Ingestion of official Census of India Table A-04 Class I to VI settlement records spanning 1901AD to 2011AD, imperial gazetteer baselines [@ImperialGazetteer1908] and South Asian primary-monograph metropolis anchors [@Habib1982Atlas; @Moosvi1987Economy; @Bayly1983Rulers], incorporating 16.552 settlements.
- Wave 2: Compilation of multi-repository archaeological and monument corpora (Pleiades, Zenodo Harappan, Vidarbha and Palaeolithic IARs, ASI P1371, Wikidata, OpenStreetMap and XRONOS/c14bazAAR) [@Possehl1999IndusAge; @Kenoyer1998AncientCities; @Allchin1995Archaeology; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation], adding 7.991 settlements (cumulative 24.543).
- Wave 3: Integration of macro-envelope *qasba*, *pargana* and *nadu* continuity series [@Hambly1982Towns; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade; @Stein1989Vijayanagara; @Eaton1993Rise; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making] with foundation-year truncation and chronological toponymy audits, contributing 3.995 settlements (cumulative 28.538).
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap hunting and GeoNames homonym resolution across all eight divisions, yielding zero unaccounted settlements and confirming asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 28.589 candidate records were audited: 28.538 were accepted as distinct settlements with longitudinal demographic series, while 51 duplicate or overlapping records were excluded.

# Results

## National Population Trajectory and Decennial Growth Pulses

Between 1947AD and 2026AD, India's population grew by 1,12B inhabitants, multiplying by a factor of 4,26 over 79 years (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

```{r fig-trajectory, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig2_india_after_independence_demography.png",
  "Demographic trajectory of the Republic of India (1947AD to 2026AD), showing national population expansion across eight macro-regions (Panel A) and the rank-size distribution of 28.538 catalogued settlements (Panel B).",
  "fig:trajectory"
)
```

```{r tbl-benchmarks, results='asis'}
bm_years <- c("1947", "1951", "1961", "1971", "1981", "1991", "2001", "2011", "2021", "2026")
bm_rows <- lapply(bm_years, function (yk) {
  tot_pop <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[[yk]])
  nth <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$ind_north_hindi_heartland$population[[yk]])
  nw <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$ind_northwest_punjab_raj$population[[yk]])
  wst <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$ind_west_maha_gujarat$population[[yk]])
  cnt <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$ind_central_mp_cg$population[[yk]])
  est <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$ind_east_wb_odisha$population[[yk]])
  ne <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$ind_northeast_eight$population[[yk]])
  sth <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$ind_south_deccan_peninsula$population[[yk]])
  isl <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$ind_islands_andaman_laksh$population[[yk]])
  dens <- tot_pop / tot_area
  data.frame(
    Benchmark = fmt_yr(yk),
    TotalPop = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_pop),
    Heartland = viscount_fmt_pop(nth),
    Northwest = viscount_fmt_pop(nw),
    West = viscount_fmt_pop(wst),
    South = viscount_fmt_pop(sth),
    Central = viscount_fmt_pop(cnt),
    East = viscount_fmt_pop(est),
    Northeast = viscount_fmt_pop(ne),
    Density = viscount_fmt_number(dens, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_bm <- do.call(rbind, bm_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_bm,
  "Decennial benchmark populations and aggregate densities across the Republic of India (1947AD to 2026AD).",
  c("Benchmark", "Total Pop", "Heartland", "Northwest", "West", "South", "Central", "East", "Northeast", "Density km⁻²"),
  list(label = "tab:benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

The trajectory exhibits three distinct demographic phases:
1. High-momentum expansion (1947AD to 1981AD): National population nearly doubled from 344M to 683,33M, adding 339,33M people in 34 years at an average decennial growth rate of 21,5% in the 1950s, 24,8% in the 1960s and 24,7% in the 1970s [@Hasmot2015India; @Chakraborty2020What].
2. Decelerating increment (1981AD to 2011AD): Although absolute decennial increments reached their historical maximum during the 1990s (adding 182,32M people between 1991AD and 2001AD), the decennial growth rate dropped steadily from 23,9% between 1981AD and 1991AD to 21,5% between 1991AD and 2001AD and 17,7% between 2001AD and 2011AD as fertility decline diffused into the Gangetic plains [@Konita2026Fertility; @James2026Silent].
3. Approaching stationary stabilisation (2011AD to 2026AD): Decennial growth fell to approximately 12% over the 2011AD to 2021AD decade and is projected to drop below 9% between 2021AD and 2031AD, reflecting sub-replacement fertility across more than two-thirds of Indian states and Union Territories [@Jain2025Populati]. In 2023AD, India surpassed mainland China to become the world's most populous country, peaking earlier and lower than projected in twentieth-century demographic models [@Gupta2023Demograp; @Qin2026Scenario].

## Sub-Regional Trajectories and Density Gradients

The spatial distribution of demographic mass shifted decisively northward over the study period. In 1947AD, the northern Hindi heartland accommodated 103,2M people (30% of national population), while the southern peninsular domain accommodated 66,74M (19,4%). By 2026AD, the northern heartland expanded to 439,5M (accounting for 30% of national population despite substantial out-migration), attaining a density of 950,51 persons per km².

The southern domain grew at a much more moderate pace, expanding from 66,74M in 1947AD to 284,21M in 2026AD (447,89 persons per km²). The western industrial littoral of Maharashtra and Gujarat experienced substantial demographic expansion driven by sustained in-migration, growing from 49,88M in 1947AD to 212,43M in 2026AD (430,25 persons per km²). The northwestern block (Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Himachal, Jammu-Kashmir, Ladakh and Rajasthan) expanded from 44,72M to 190,45M (322,58 persons per km²), with high growth concentrated in the National Capital Region and eastern Rajasthan.

The eastern division (West Bengal and Odisha) expanded from 37,84M to 161,15M, reaching an elevated density of 673,59 persons per km² along the lower Gangetic plain and coastal deltas. The central uplands (Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh) grew from 28,21M to 120,13M (269,28 persons per km²), while the northeastern states expanded from 13,07M to 55,67M (215,52 persons per km²).

## Urban Agglomeration and the Census Town Phenomenon

India's urban population expanded from 62,4M in 1951AD (17,3% of total population) to 377,1M in 2011AD (31,2%), and is estimated at over 530M in 2026AD (approximately 36,2%). This urban transition displayed a pronounced dual character [@Jain2018Contempo].

At the apex of the settlement hierarchy, prime metropolises evolved into sprawling megacity regions. Mumbai, anchored by the island city and Thane-Navi Mumbai conurbations, expanded from 3,22M in 1951AD to 18,39M in 2011AD and 22,35M (22.347.507) in 2025AD. Delhi, building upon the historic urban core of Shahjahanabad [@Blake1991Shahjahanabad; @Naqvi1968Urbanisation], grew from 1,44M in 1951AD to 16,35M in 2011AD and 19,86M (19.862.991) in 2025AD across its urban agglomeration. Kolkata expanded from 4,69M in 1951AD to 14,06M in 2011AD and 17,08M (17.078.693) in 2025AD. In the south, Chennai grew from 1,54M in 1951AD to 8,65M in 2011AD and 10,51M (10.512.941) in 2025AD, technology-driven expansion propelled Bengaluru from 786k in 1951AD to 8,52M in 2011AD and 10,35M (10.351.258) in 2025AD, and Hyderabad grew from 1,14M in 1951AD to 7,68M in 2011AD and 9,33M (9.326.612) in 2025AD. Major western industrial nodes followed closely, with Ahmedabad expanding from 925k in 1951AD to 6,36M in 2011AD and 7,72M (7.723.798) in 2025AD, and Pune rising from 609k in 1951AD to 5,06M in 2011AD and 6,14M (6.144.481) in 2025AD.

Concurrently, the Census of 2011AD revealed a dramatic surge in census towns: settlements meeting urban demographic criteria (population over 5.000, density over 400 persons per km² and more than 75% of male main workers in non-agricultural pursuits) that remain governed as rural panchayats [@Jain2018Contempo]. The number of census towns surged from 1.362 in 2001AD to 3.894 in 2011AD, accounting for nearly 30% of total urban growth during the decade. This phenomenon reflects widespread sub-metropolitan economic diversification, wherein rural households transition out of agriculture into small-scale trade, transport and construction without physical migration to major metropolises [@Jain2018Contempo].

# Limitations

## Boundary Reorganisation and District Splitting

Reconstructing historical population series across eight decades is subject to methodological limitations arising from frequent administrative boundary modifications. Between 1951AD and 2011AD, the number of administrative districts in India increased from 311 to 640 through continuous administrative bifurcation and trifurcation. While our macro-regional aggregations remain robust to internal district splitting, boundary harmonisation across former princely states and restructured provincial frontiers introduces small spatial allocation variances in early intercensal periods.

## Post-2011 Enumeration Hiatus and Contemporary Projections

The postponement of the decennial Census of 2021AD represents an unprecedented data hiatus in modern Indian demographic history. For the first time since 1881AD, a decennial census was not conducted on schedule. Consequently, benchmark estimates for 2021AD and 2026AD rely on demographic projection models, vital statistics from the Sample Registration System and electoral roll counts rather than universal house-to-house enumeration. Although national totals are constrained within narrow uncertainty bounds (+/- 2,5%), fine-grained municipal and ward-level population trajectories for newly formed peri-urban settlements carry wider margins of error.

# Conclusion

The post-independence demographic transition of the Republic of India constitutes an unprecedented spatial and societal transformation. Between 1947AD and 2026AD, national population expanded more than fourfold from 344M to 1,47B, while crude death rates fell by more than 70% and life expectancy more than doubled. This expansion unfolded across profound geographic contrasts: early fertility transition and rapid economic modernisation stabilised the southern peninsular states, while youthful demographic momentum concentrated unprecedented human numbers in the alluvial northern heartland.

By integrating 28.538 catalogued settlements with dasymetrically disaggregated rural surfaces, this study demonstrates that India's contemporary urban transition is characterised as much by the diffused growth of intermediate census towns and rural diversification as by metropolitan primacy. As India's total fertility rate settles below replacement level in the mid-2020s, the nation stands at the threshold of a new demographic era, transitioning from rapid expansion toward eventual population peaking and structural ageing.

# Appendix

## Mathematical Formulation of Boundary Feathering

To eliminate step discontinuities across macro-regional boundaries during dasymetric allocation, a two-pass Gaussian boundary feathering kernel is applied to the rural density surface:
$$\tilde{\rho}(x, y) = \frac{\sum_{i=-k}^{k} \sum_{j=-k}^{k} w(i, j) \rho(x+i, y+j)}{\sum_{i=-k}^{k} \sum_{j=-k}^{k} w(i, j)}$$
where $w(i, j) = \exp\left(-\frac{i^2 + j^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$ with bandwidth $\sigma = 1,5$ grid cells (approximately 13,8 km), restricted strictly to cells within 30 km of regional frontiers to preserve internal sub-regional population mass.

## Decennial Growth Rates across Macro-Regions

Table \ref{tab:growth} documents decennial compound annual growth rates across the eight macro-regions from 1951AD to 2026AD.

```{r tbl-growth, results='asis'}
calc_cagr <- function (p0, p1, dt) {
  if (p0 <= 0 || p1 <= 0 || dt <= 0) return(0)
  ((p1 / p0)^(1 / dt) - 1) * 100
}

periods <- list(
  c("1951", "1961", 10),
  c("1961", "1971", 10),
  c("1971", "1981", 10),
  c("1981", "1991", 10),
  c("1991", "2001", 10),
  c("2001", "2011", 10),
  c("2011", "2026", 15)
)

growth_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  r <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  cagrs <- vapply(periods, function (prd) {
    p0 <- as.numeric(r$population[[prd[1]]])
    p1 <- as.numeric(r$population[[prd[2]]])
    dt <- as.numeric(prd[3])
    calc_cagr(p0, p1, dt)
  }, numeric(1))
  data.frame(
    Region = if (!is.null(reg_short[[rk]])) reg_short[[rk]] else clean_text(r$name),
    G1951_61 = viscount_fmt_number(cagrs[1], 2L),
    G1961_71 = viscount_fmt_number(cagrs[2], 2L),
    G1971_81 = viscount_fmt_number(cagrs[3], 2L),
    G1981_91 = viscount_fmt_number(cagrs[4], 2L),
    G1991_01 = viscount_fmt_number(cagrs[5], 2L),
    G2001_11 = viscount_fmt_number(cagrs[6], 2L),
    G2011_26 = viscount_fmt_number(cagrs[7], 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_growth <- do.call(rbind, growth_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_growth,
  "Decennial compound annual population growth rates (%) across macro-regions (1951AD to 2026AD).",
  c("Macro-Region", "1951-61", "1961-71", "1971-81", "1981-91", "1991-01", "2001-11", "2011-26"),
  list(label = "tab:growth", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```
